events.title: Early Stone Age Inhabitants
events.description: Early humans in the Central African Republic region used stone tools, living by hunting and gathering. Archaeological evidence shows this area had rich natural resources and early human activities. These societies were small-scale, highly mobile, adapted to local environment.

events.title: Early Human Settlement
events.description: Archaeological evidence shows human activity in Central African region during Neolithic period. Hunter-gatherers in Ubangi and Chari river basins established early settlements. These early inhabitants used stone tools, engaged in hunting, fishing and gathering. Central Africa's tropical rainforests and savanna regions provided rich resources for early humans.

events.title: Bantu Migration Begins
events.description: Bantu-speaking peoples began migrating from West Africa into Central African region, bringing agricultural techniques and iron-working knowledge. This massive migration transformed Central Africa's demographic and cultural landscape. Bantu introduced tuber crop cultivation, pottery making and more advanced tool manufacturing. They gradually replaced or assimilated indigenous Pygmy populations.

events.title: Agricultural Society Development
events.description: Agricultural technology further developed in Central African region, settled farming became primary lifestyle. People cultivated sorghum, millet and tuber crops, developing crop rotation and land management techniques. Village sizes expanded, specialized craft production emerged including pottery, textiles and iron-working. Livestock raising included goats, sheep and poultry. Social organization became more stable, clan and family systems strengthened.

events.title: Early Kingdom and Chiefdom Formation
events.description: The Central African Republic region began showing more complex political structures, including chiefdoms and small kingdoms. These political entities were based on agriculture, trade, and military power. Chiefs consolidated power through controlling iron production, mediating disputes and organizing defense. Hereditary rule and hierarchical social structures emerged.

events.title: Sao Civilization Influence
events.description: Though Sao civilization mainly located in Lake Chad region, its influence extended to northern parts of today's Central African Republic. Sao people renowned for exquisite bronze and pottery craftsmanship. They established complex social structures and trade networks, trading with North Africa and Nile Valley. Sao cultural sites discovered in northern CAR prove cross-regional cultural exchange.

events.title: Regional Trade Development
events.description: Central African region gradually integrated into broader African trade networks. Local goods like ivory, animal skins, honey and iron products were traded to northern and eastern markets. Salt, beads and cloth from Sahel regions flowed into Central Africa. Trade routes developed along major rivers, promoting cultural exchange and new technology spread. Some villages prospered due to location on trade routes.

events.title: Trade Network Expansion
events.description: The region's trade networks further developed, connecting to broader Africa and trans-Saharan regions. Commodities included gold, salt, ivory, and slaves. This brought wealth and cultural exchange.

events.title: Banda and Nzakara Settlement
events.description: Banda and Nzakara peoples became major ethnic groups in Central African region, establishing scattered chiefdoms and villages. These groups developed complex social organizations, religious beliefs and artistic traditions. They engaged in agriculture, hunting and regional trade. Banda particularly renowned for blacksmith skills and musical traditions. This period formed CAR's basic ethnic pattern.

events.title: Trans-Saharan Trade Routes
events.description: Central African region became part of trans-Saharan trade network, though in peripheral position. Ivory, slaves and other goods transported via northern routes to North African and Middle Eastern markets. These trade connections brought Islamic influence, especially in northern regions. Trade also promoted wealth accumulation and political power concentration.

events.title: Slave Trade Era
events.description: Central African region deeply affected by Atlantic and trans-Saharan slave trades. Though far from coast, region became source for slave capture. Powerful neighboring kingdoms like Darfur Sultanate and Wadai Empire conducted slave raids into Central Africa. This caused population decline, social disruption and persistent insecurity. Many villages destroyed, survivors fled into deep forests. Slave trade had devastating impact on CAR's population and social development.

events.title: Firearms Trade and Power Shifts
events.description: European firearms gradually entered Central African region through North African trade routes. Chiefdoms possessing firearms gained military advantages, able to expand territories and conduct more effective slave raids. This led to power structure reorganization, some traditionally strong groups declined while those acquiring weapons rose. Firearms trade intensified regional conflicts and instability.

events.title: Bornu and Wadai Influence
events.description: Bornu Empire and Wadai Sultanate from north expanded influence into northern Central African region. These Islamic states conducted regular slave raiding expeditions, severely disrupting local societies. They established trading posts and tributary relationships. During this period northern CAR gradually Islamized while south maintained traditional beliefs. Continuous raiding left region in chaos and poverty.

events.title: Rabih az-Zubayr's Conquest
events.description: Sudanese warlord Rabih az-Zubayr established empire spanning Chad and northern CAR. His army equipped with modern weapons, conducted brutal conquests and slave raids. Rabih built military state based on slave trade, capital at N'Djamena (then Kousséri). His rule characterized by violence and terror, causing massive destruction in CAR. Rabih's empire ended only when defeated by French forces in 1900.

events.title: European Explorers Arrive
events.description: European explorers began exploring Central African interior. Belgian explorers explored Ubangi River basin for King Leopold II. French explorer Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza explored Congo and Ubangi river regions. These expeditions paved way for subsequent colonial conquest. Explorer reports described region's resources and strategic importance.

events.title: French Colonial Expansion Begins
events.description: France began establishing colonial outposts in Ubangi River region. In 1889 France established first permanent post at Bangui. France expanded territory through signing 'protection' treaties with local chiefs. These treaties often obtained through coercion or deception. France faced resistance from local inhabitants but gradually conquered region with superior weapons.

events.title: Oubangui-Chari Territory Established
events.description: France formally established Oubangui-Chari colonial territory, predecessor of today's Central African Republic. Territory named after Ubangi and Chari rivers. Bangui designated as capital. France began establishing colonial administrative system, but actual control limited to major river areas. Interior regions remained largely uncontrolled.

events.title: Early Colonial Resistance
events.description: Local chiefs and villages conducted sporadic resistance against French colonial expansion. Many Banda and Gbaya leaders refused to sign protection treaties, organizing armed resistance against French military expeditions. France used 'pacification' tactics, burning resistant villages, executing leaders. Despite inferior weapons, local warriors used terrain and guerrilla tactics creating difficulties for French forces. However, French superior firepower eventually suppressed most resistance.

events.title: Battle Against Rabih
events.description: French forces engaged in decisive battle with Rabih az-Zubayr's army in Lake Chad region. On April 22, 1900, in Battle of Kousséri, Rabih defeated and killed. This victory enabled France to consolidate control over northern CAR. However, Rabih's followers continued resistance for years. This battle marked crucial turning point in French colonial rule in CAR.

events.title: Concessionary Company Exploitation
events.description: France leased most of Oubangui-Chari to private concessionary companies, granting them monopoly rights over rubber and ivory. These companies brutally exploited local population, forcing them to collect rubber and ivory. Those refusing or failing to meet quotas suffered torture, mutilation or death. Villages burned, hostages taken. This period called 'Red Rubber' era, caused massive death and suffering. Estimated hundreds of thousands died from abuse, starvation and disease.

events.title: Forced Labor System Established
events.description: French colonial authorities formally implemented forced labor system (corvée). All adult males required to provide several weeks unpaid labor annually for road construction, porterage and public works. Refusers faced imprisonment, fines or corporal punishment. This system severely disrupted agricultural production and family life, causing widespread suffering. Many attempted to flee to remote areas to avoid forced labor.

events.title: French Equatorial Africa Formed
events.description: Oubangui-Chari became part of newly formed French Equatorial Africa (AEF) federation, together with Gabon, Middle Congo and Chad. Federation capital at Brazzaville. This administrative reorganization aimed to improve colonial rule efficiency. However, Oubangui-Chari remained poorest, most neglected territory in federation.

events.title: Kongo-Wara Rebellion
events.description: Banda leader Kongo-Wara led major uprising against French colonial rule and concessionary company atrocities. Rebellion lasted from 1911 to 1917, involving tens of thousands of fighters. Kongo-Wara's forces used guerrilla tactics, attacking French posts and company facilities. France deployed large forces for brutal suppression, burning villages, massacring civilians. Kongo-Wara finally captured and executed in 1917. This uprising symbolizes CAR's anti-colonial resistance.

events.title: Congo-Ocean Railway Construction
events.description: France forced tens of thousands of Central African laborers to participate in building Congo-Ocean Railway connecting Brazzaville to Atlantic coast. Working conditions extremely harsh, workers suffered abuse, starvation and disease. Estimated over 17,000 workers died during construction, many from Oubangui-Chari. This project called 'Death Railway,' became another dark chapter of colonial exploitation.

events.title: Kongo-Wara Uprising
events.description: Gbaya people launched uprising in Kongo-Wara region against forced labor and taxation. Uprising led by traditional leader Karnu, gained widespread support. French forces conducted brutal suppression, using aircraft to bomb villages. Thousands killed, many villages destroyed. This uprising reflected widespread discontent under colonial rule.

events.title: Forced Cotton Cultivation
events.description: France implemented forced cotton cultivation system in Oubangui-Chari. Farmers forced to grow cotton instead of food crops, selling at low prices to French companies. This caused food shortages and famine. Those refusing to grow cotton faced punishment. This policy severely disrupted traditional agriculture and food security, causing long-term economic hardship.

events.title: Head Tax and Monetary Economy
events.description: French colonial authorities enforced head tax collection, requiring payment in French currency. This forced subsistence farmers into cash economy, having to sell labor or agricultural products to obtain money. Many forced into seasonal migrant labor, traveling to plantations in Congo or Cameroon. This policy disrupted traditional economic systems, intensifying social disintegration. Tax collection process often accompanied by violence and corruption.

events.title: Joining Free France
events.description: After the fall of France, Félix Éboué, the governor-general of French Equatorial Africa (himself a Black man), declared his support for de Gaulle's Free French movement and refused to recognize the Vichy regime. Ubangi-Shari became an important base for Free France. This decision made French Equatorial Africa the principal Free French stronghold in Africa and was vital to the Allied war effort.

events.title: WWII Contributions
events.description: Oubangui-Chari made significant contributions to Allied war effort. Thousands of Central Africans conscripted, fighting in North African and European theaters. Territory provided important raw materials and supplies. However, war intensified forced labor and economic exploitation. Many Central African soldiers killed or wounded in combat. After war, veterans became important force in nationalist movement.

events.title: Became French Overseas Territory
events.description: Post-war, Oubangui-Chari's status changed from colony to French overseas territory, theoretically enjoying more autonomy. Forced labor officially abolished (though actually continued). Central Africans gained limited political rights, including right to elect representatives to French parliament. However, suffrage limited to small educated elite.

events.title: Barthélemy Boganda Elected
events.description: Barthélemy Boganda elected as Oubangui-Chari's representative to French National Assembly, becoming dominant figure in Central African politics. Boganda was charismatic leader, former Catholic priest turned politician. He advocated for Central African people's rights and greater autonomy. Boganda founded Movement for Social Evolution of Black Africa (MESAN), becoming main nationalist party.

events.title: Post-War Economic Hardship
events.description: After WWII, Oubangui-Chari faced severe economic difficulties. Infrastructure dilapidated, productivity low, population reduced by war conscription and forced labor. French investment limited, mainly focused on resource extraction. Most population lived in poverty, lacking education and healthcare services. This period's economic stagnation laid groundwork for later political instability. Only very few Africans received formal education.

events.title: Nationalist Consciousness Awakening
events.description: Educated Central African elite began organizing political activities, demanding more rights and autonomy. Boganda's MESAN party became center of nationalist movement. African intellectuals discussed independence, Pan-Africanism and decolonization. However, colonial authorities strictly limited political activities, surveilling and harassing nationalists. Nevertheless, desire for independence gradually grew among people.

events.title: Loi Cadre Framework Law
events.description: France passed Loi Cadre (Framework Law), granting African colonies limited internal autonomy. Oubangui-Chari established territorial assembly, expanded suffrage. This marked beginning of transition from direct colonial rule to autonomy. However, France retained control over foreign affairs, defense and important economic sectors. These reforms viewed as insufficient, but opened space for political participation.

events.title: Mysterious Death of Boganda
events.description: Barthélemy Boganda died mysteriously in a plane crash when his aircraft went down on the way back to Bangui. Many suspected that French intelligence had arranged his assassination, since Boganda was increasingly inclined toward full independence. His death shocked all of Central Africa and set off mass protests and unrest. Boganda became a national hero and martyr, and his legacy still shapes Central African politics today.

events.title: Founding of the Autonomous Republic
events.description: After de Gaulle's referendum on the constitution of the Fifth Republic, Ubangi-Shari became an autonomous republic within the French Community and was renamed the Central African Republic. Boganda's nephew David Dacko became the first prime minister. Although still under French influence, this marked an important step toward full independence. The Central African Republic began to build its own government institutions and administrative system.

events.title: Independence of the Central African Republic
events.description: The Central African Republic formally declared independence, with David Dacko as its first president. Independence celebrations were held in Bangui, but the mood was dimmed by Boganda's absence. The country joined the United Nations and the Organization of African Unity. However, the new state inherited serious problems from the colonial period: poverty, a lack of infrastructure, low levels of education, and ethnic divisions. France retained strong economic and military influence.

events.title: Dacko's Authoritarian Rule
events.description: President Dacko gradually established authoritarian rule, banning opposition parties, turning MESAN into one-party state tool. He relied on French support to maintain power. Dacko government corrupt and inefficient, failed to address nation's economic and social problems. Civil servant salaries often delayed, public services deteriorated. Discontent grew in military and population.

events.title: Bokassa's Coup
events.description: Colonel Jean-Bédel Bokassa, Dacko's cousin and the army chief of staff, overthrew Dacko in a bloodless coup, seizing power while Dacko was abroad. Bokassa proclaimed himself president, promising to end corruption and restore order. The coup was supported by the army and by many ordinary people. Bokassa dissolved the National Assembly, suspended the constitution, and began a rule that would last thirteen years.

events.title: Bokassa Presidential Period
events.description: Bokassa ruled CAR as President, establishing personal dictatorship. He concentrated power, brutally suppressed opposition, often personally participating in torture and executions. Bokassa's rule characterized by capriciousness, violence and extravagance. He maintained close relations with France, especially personal friendship with French President Giscard d'Estaing. Despite French aid, economy continued deteriorating, corruption rampant.

events.title: Founding of the Central African Empire
events.description: Bokassa declared the Central African Republic an empire and crowned himself Emperor Bokassa I. He claimed that this was to restore Africa's traditional monarchy. The international community generally regarded the move as absurd and megalomaniacal. Imitating Napoleon, Bokassa planned a grand coronation ceremony.

events.title: The Lavish Coronation
events.description: Bokassa held an extremely lavish coronation modeled on Napoleon's. The ceremony cost about 20 million US dollars, equivalent to one third of the national annual budget. Bokassa wore a velvet robe studded with pearls and diamonds and a golden crown weighing 5 kilograms. France provided most of the funds. The extravagant ceremony, held in one of the poorest countries in the world, drew international condemnation and ridicule.

events.title: Student Protests
events.description: Students in Bangui protested against being forced to buy expensive school uniforms produced by factories owned by Bokassa. Bokassa ordered the army to suppress the protests, leading to the arrest of hundreds of students. Many students were tortured in prison, and some were killed. The incident attracted international attention and condemnation.

events.title: Massacre of Children
events.description: About 100 imprisoned schoolchildren were killed in Ngaragba Prison. Bokassa was reported to have taken part in the massacre personally. The atrocity was confirmed by an African commission of inquiry and provoked intense outrage in the international community. Even France, Bokassa's supporter, could no longer defend him. The incident became the catalyst for his overthrow.

events.title: Operation Barracuda: Bokassa Overthrown
events.description: While Bokassa was visiting Libya, France launched Operation Barracuda, sending paratroopers to overthrow him and restore former president Dacko. The operation was swift and met almost no resistance. Bokassa went into exile in Côte d'Ivoire and later in France. The empire was abolished and the country reverted to being the Central African Republic. Dacko promised democratic reforms but faced a country ravaged by Bokassa's rule.

events.title: Dacko's Second Term
events.description: Dacko restored to presidency, attempted to rebuild nation. He faced enormous challenges: collapsed economy, empty treasury, demoralized civil service and traumatized population. Dacko relied on French aid but failed to govern effectively. Corruption continued, economy didn't improve. Dacko's health deteriorated, he increasingly relied on advisors. Political instability persisted.

events.title: Kolingba's Coup
events.description: General André Kolingba, the army chief of staff, overthrew Dacko in a bloodless coup and set up a military committee. Kolingba promised to end corruption, restore the economy, and eventually achieve democracy. The coup was supported by the army and by many people weary of Dacko's incompetent rule. Kolingba suspended the constitution, dissolved political institutions, and began a rule that would last 22 years.

events.title: Kolingba Military Rule
events.description: Kolingba ruled CAR as military strongman, though milder than Bokassa, still authoritarian rule. He established one-party system, creating Central African Democratic Rally (RDC) as sole legal party. Kolingba suppressed opposition, controlled media, but avoided Bokassa-style extreme violence. Economy slightly improved in 1980s but remained poor. Kolingba maintained good relations with France and other Western countries, receiving aid.

events.title: Bokassa Returns for Trial
events.description: Exiled Bokassa unexpectedly returned to CAR, immediately arrested. In 1987 he tried for murder, embezzlement and other crimes, including cannibalism charges (unproven). Trial attracted international attention. Bokassa sentenced to death, later commuted to life imprisonment. He spent several years in prison, released in 1993, died in 1996.

events.title: Democratization Pressure
events.description: With Cold War ending and African democratization wave, Kolingba faced domestic and international pressure for democratic reforms. Students, unions and emerging civil society organizations held protests and strikes. France and other donors linked aid to political reforms. Kolingba initially resisted but eventually forced to make concessions.

events.title: Multi-party System Restored
events.description: Under sustained pressure, Kolingba announced restoration of multi-party system, ending one-party rule. Opposition parties allowed to form, press freedom expanded. National conference convened to discuss political transition. However, Kolingba tried to control reform process, maintain power. Political opening led to intense partisan competition and social tensions.

events.title: First Democratic Elections
events.description: CAR held first multi-party presidential and parliamentary elections. After 1992 first round voting, 1993 held runoff. Ange-Félix Patassé defeated Kolingba to become President, ending Kolingba's 12-year rule. Elections though flawed, considered basically free and fair. This marked important milestone in CAR democratization. Patassé promised reforms and national reconciliation.

events.title: Patassé Presidency
events.description: Patassé's rule filled with turbulence and instability. He faced economic crisis, civil servant salary arrears and military discontent. Patassé relied on ethnic support, exacerbating ethnic tensions. His government corrupt and incompetent, failed to improve livelihoods. Patassé's relations with opposition and military deteriorated, leading to multiple mutinies and coup attempts.

events.title: Military Mutinies
events.description: CAR military launched three mutinies (April, May and November 1996) due to salary arrears and poor conditions. Mutinous soldiers controlled parts of Bangui, fighting with loyal forces. French troops intervened, helping restore order. Mutinies caused hundreds of deaths, thousands displaced. African mediation led to establishment of African peacekeeping force (MISAB), later replaced by UN mission (MINURCA).

events.title: UN Peacekeeping Operation
events.description: UN Mission in Central African Republic (MINURCA) deployed, helping stabilize situation, supervise disarmament and prepare elections. This was UN's first major peacekeeping operation in CAR. MINURCA achieved some success, helping restore relative calm. Mission withdrew in 2000, but root causes of instability unresolved.

events.title: Patassé Re-elected
events.description: In controversial election, Patassé won re-election. Opposition alleged fraud and irregularities. General Kolingba came second. Election exacerbated political tensions and ethnic divisions. Patassé's second term continued filled with crises and instability. Economy continued deteriorating, security situation fragile.

events.title: Coup Attempts
events.description: General Kolingba and his supporters attempted multiple times to overthrow Patassé. Failed coups occurred in May 2001 and October 2002. Patassé accused Kolingba of plotting coups, Kolingba fled to Democratic Republic of Congo. Political crisis deepened, violence increased. Patassé increasingly relied on foreign mercenaries, especially armed groups from Chad and Libya to protect himself.

events.title: Bozizé's Coup
events.description: General François Bozizé, the former army chief of staff, launched a coup while Patassé was abroad and occupied Bangui. Bozizé was backed by Chadian troops. Patassé went into exile in Togo. Bozizé suspended the constitution, dissolved the government, and promised a transition to democracy. The coup was welcomed by many Central Africans weary of Patassé's rule, but it also raised international concern about the breach of constitutional order.

events.title: Bozizé Transitional Government
events.description: Bozizé established transitional government, promising elections within two years. He tried to restore order, improve relations with international community. However, security situation remained fragile, rebellions emerged in northern and eastern regions. Bozizé relied on French and Chadian support. Economy remained difficult, basic services lacking.

events.title: Northern Rebellions Rise
events.description: Multiple rebel groups emerged in northern and eastern regions opposing Bozizé government. Major groups included Popular Front for the Recovery of Central African Republic (FDPC) and People's Army for the Restoration of Democracy (APRD). Rebels accused Bozizé of dictatorship, corruption and ethnic discrimination. Conflict caused tens of thousands displaced, humanitarian crisis worsened. Violence by government forces, rebels and bandit groups affected civilians.

events.title: Bozizé Elected President
events.description: In 2005 elections, Bozizé elected President with 64% of vote, legitimizing his rule. Opposition alleged unfair elections, but international observers considered elections basically acceptable. Bozizé promised reconciliation, development and security. However, his government continued facing challenges of rebellion, corruption and poor governance.

events.title: Peace Agreements and Continued Conflict
events.description: Government signed peace agreements with major rebel groups, promising disarmament, demobilization and reintegration (DDR). However, agreements poorly implemented, many rebels refused to disarm. New armed groups emerged, violence continued. Northern and eastern regions remained unstable, government control weak.

events.title: Humanitarian Crisis Worsens
events.description: Continued conflict led to serious humanitarian crisis. Hundreds of thousands displaced, many fled to neighboring countries. Civilians suffered violence from government forces, rebels and bandits, including killings, rape and looting. Humanitarian organizations struggled to access affected areas. Food insecurity and disease spread. International attention limited, CAR called 'forgotten crisis.'

events.title: Bozizé Re-elected
events.description: In controversial election, Bozizé won re-election with about 64% of vote. Opposition boycotted election, alleging fraud and unfair conditions. Turnout low. Bozizé's re-election consolidated his power but failed to address nation's fundamental problems. Corruption rampant, economy stagnant, security situation deteriorating. Discontent grew in military and population.

events.title: Start of the Séléka Rebellion
events.description: A rebel coalition called Séléka (meaning "alliance") launched an offensive in the north and quickly captured several towns. Séléka was made up mainly of Muslims and accused Bozizé of failing to honor peace agreements, of corruption, and of marginalizing the northern region. The rebels were led by Michel Djotodia and were supported by Chadian and Sudanese mercenaries. Government forces were unable to resist, and Séléka advanced rapidly.

events.title: Libreville Agreement
events.description: Under the mediation of the Economic Community of Central African States (ECCAS), the government and Séléka signed a peace agreement in Libreville, Gabon. The agreement provided for a unity government and for Séléka to disarm. Nicolas Tiangaye was appointed prime minister. However, the agreement soon collapsed, as Séléka accused Bozizé of failing to keep his promises and continued its offensive.

events.title: Séléka Captures Bangui
events.description: Séléka rebels entered the capital, Bangui, and overthrew President Bozizé. After brief fighting, Bozizé fled to Cameroon and later to Benin. Séléka leader Michel Djotodia declared himself president. The coup drew international condemnation, and the Central African Republic was suspended from the African Union. Séléka soldiers carried out looting and violence in Bangui, causing panic.

events.title: Séléka Atrocities and the Rise of the Anti-Balaka
events.description: Djotodia was formally sworn in as president but could not control the Séléka fighters. Séléka soldiers committed large-scale atrocities across the country: killing, rape, looting, and the destruction of villages, mainly targeting Christian civilians. In response, a Christian militia known as the Anti-Balaka (meaning "anti-machete") arose and carried out retaliatory attacks on Muslims. The Central African Republic descended into sectarian violence, with thousands killed and hundreds of thousands displaced. The international community warned of the risk of genocide.

events.title: French Operation Sangaris
events.description: France launched Operation Sangaris, sending 1,600 soldiers to support the African-led International Support Mission (MISCA). French forces tried to separate the warring factions, protect civilians, and restore order. However, violence continued to escalate, especially in Bangui, where fierce fighting between Séléka and the Anti-Balaka left hundreds dead.

events.title: Djotodia Resigns
events.description: Under pressure from regional leaders, Djotodia resigned the presidency and went into exile in Benin. Séléka was formally dissolved, but many former fighters refused to disarm. Catherine Samba-Panza was appointed transitional president, becoming the first female head of state of the Central African Republic. She promised to restore peace and reconciliation but faced enormous challenges.

events.title: Djotodia Resigns
events.description: Under regional leaders' pressure, Djotodia resigned as President, fled to Benin. Séléka formally dissolved, but many former fighters refused to disarm. Catherine Samba-Panza appointed transitional President, becoming CAR's first female head of state. She promised to restore peace and reconciliation but faced enormous challenges.

events.title: Deployment of UN Peacekeepers
events.description: The United Nations Multidimensional Integrated Stabilization Mission in the Central African Republic (MINUSCA) took over from MISCA, deploying about 12,000 peacekeepers. MINUSCA's mandate included protecting civilians, supporting the political transition, promoting human rights, and providing humanitarian assistance. However, the peacekeepers faced enormous challenges: vast territory, numerous armed groups, limited resources, and complex conflict dynamics.

events.title: Political Transition
events.description: Under international support, CAR underwent political transition process. December 2015 held constitutional referendum, adopting new constitution. 2015-2016 held presidential and parliamentary elections. Former Prime Minister Faustin-Archange Touadéra defeated former Prime Minister Anicet-Georges Dologuélé in runoff to become President. Touadéra was mathematics professor, viewed as moderate technocrat. Elections though flawed and violent, considered important step in restoring constitutional order.

events.title: Touadéra's Inauguration
events.description: Faustin-Archange Touadéra took office as president, ending the transition period. He promised reconciliation, disarmament, and the rebuilding of the country. Touadéra faced a daunting task: most of the country was controlled by armed groups, the economy had collapsed, basic services were lacking, and the population was traumatized. He called on armed groups to lay down their weapons and take part in the peace process.

events.title: Violence Escalates and Armed Groups Proliferate
events.description: Despite new government, violence actually escalated. Former Séléka split into multiple factions, fighting each other for territory and resources. Anti-Balaka also fragmented into numerous groups. Armed groups controlled about 80% of territory, engaged in illegal mining, timber smuggling, cattle theft and extortion. Civilians continued suffering violence, including killings, sexual violence and forced displacement. Humanitarian situation worsened, millions needed aid.

events.title: Khartoum Peace Agreement
events.description: Through the efforts of the African Union, the United Nations, and other mediators, the government and 14 armed groups signed a peace agreement in Khartoum, Sudan. The agreement included power sharing, the integration of armed groups into the security forces, amnesty, and local governance reforms. It was seen as a major breakthrough toward ending the conflict. However, many doubted its viability, since previous agreements had all failed.

events.title: Peace Agreement Implementation Difficulties
events.description: Khartoum Agreement implementation faced major challenges. Many armed groups failed to fulfill commitments, continued controlling territory and engaging in illegal activities. Violence persisted, especially in central and eastern regions. Government lacked resources and capacity to implement agreement. Some armed group leaders appointed to government positions, but this didn't bring substantial peace. Civilians continued suffering.

events.title: Touadéra Re-elected
events.description: In a disputed election, Touadéra won re-election in the first round with 53 percent of the vote, avoiding a runoff. The election took place amid serious security challenges, and many areas were unable to vote. The opposition alleged fraud and refused to accept the result. Former president Bozizé was accused of plotting a coup and fled Bangui. The election heightened political tension.

events.title: Offensive of the Coalition of Patriots for Change
events.description: Around the election, six major armed groups formed the Coalition of Patriots for Change (CPC), reportedly linked to Bozizé, and launched a large-scale offensive seeking to overthrow Touadéra's government and block the election. The CPC captured several towns and encircled Bangui. The government, backed by Rwandan forces and Russian mercenaries (the Wagner Group), counterattacked and gradually regained lost ground. The fighting caused a new wave of displacement and a humanitarian crisis.

events.title: Russian Influence Expands
events.description: Russia dramatically increased presence in CAR through Wagner Group mercenaries. Hundreds of Russian military instructors and mercenaries helped government forces fight rebels, recapture most territory. In return, Russian companies gained mining and other economic concessions. Russia also provided weapons and political support. This marked CAR's shift from traditional ally France toward Russia, raising Western concerns. Wagner accused of human rights violations.

events.title: Government Recaptures Territory
events.description: With Russian and Rwandan support, government forces recaptured most territory from CPC, including major towns and strategic locations. By early 2022, government claimed control of most territory. However, armed groups remained active in remote areas, conducting guerrilla warfare and attacks. Military victory didn't translate to lasting peace, civilians continued suffering violence.

events.title: Constitutional Referendum and Power Concentration
events.description: Touadéra held constitutional referendum, proposing constitutional amendments to remove presidential term limits, allowing him to run indefinitely. Referendum held under controversial circumstances, opposition and civil society boycotted. Official results showed overwhelming support, but turnout low with fraud allegations. New constitution also strengthened presidential powers. This move raised concerns about democratic backsliding and Touadéra's authoritarian tendencies.

events.title: Ongoing Humanitarian Crisis
events.description: Despite military progress, CAR still faces severe humanitarian crisis. About 3.4 million people (over half population) need humanitarian aid. Hundreds of thousands remain displaced, many refugees in neighboring countries. Food insecurity severe, malnutrition rates high. Basic services like healthcare and education severely inadequate. Humanitarian workers face security threats and access restrictions. International aid funding insufficient, CAR continues being one of world's most neglected crises.

events.title: Wagner Atrocity Allegations
events.description: UN and human rights organizations documented serious human rights violations committed by Russian Wagner Group mercenaries and CAR government forces, including extrajudicial executions, torture, sexual violence and looting. Civilian communities suffered retaliatory attacks. UN experts called for investigation of possible war crimes and crimes against humanity. However, Touadéra government denied allegations, continued relying on Russian support. International community's attention and influence limited.

events.title: Fragile Stability
events.description: CAR in state of fragile stability. Government with Russian support controls major towns and roads, but armed groups remain active in many rural areas. Violence levels decreased but conflict far from over. Economy remains collapsed, CAR one of world's poorest countries, ranking bottom in Human Development Index. Corruption rampant, governance weak, rule of law absent. Touadéra consolidated power but failed to achieve genuine reconciliation or development. Country dependent on foreign support, especially Russia, raising concerns about sovereignty and human rights. CAR's future remains uncertain, facing ongoing security, humanitarian and governance challenges. International engagement limited, country continues largely forgotten by world.

events.title: Iron Age Cultures
events.description: The Central African region entered the Iron Age, and the spread of ironworking promoted agricultural development and increasingly complex social organization. Archaeological sites show larger settlements and trade networks emerging in this period. Iron tools raised agricultural productivity and made population growth possible. This period also saw the formation of early political organization.
